title: AI in the Workplace: What Changes When AI Becomes a Coworker?
description: 75-minute facilitated workplace AI session combining individual judgment, team analysis, and completion of the AI in the Workplace discussion.

steps.label: 👋 ARRIVAL
steps.title: AI in the Workplace
steps.lead: What changes when AI becomes part of the team?
steps.studentTask: Join the session. Keep this page open. Then look up.

runbook.say: Today we are looking at AI as a workplace issue, not just a tool issue. Your job is to decide who benefits, who may be disadvantaged, and what responsible human judgment looks like.
runbook.askNext: When AI enters a workplace, what changes besides productivity?
runbook.watchFor: Students naming fairness, pressure, monitoring, skill changes, accountability, privacy, or access—not only speed.
runbook.advanceWhen: Students are in the room and you have 2–3 initial ideas.
runbook.landHere: AI changes work, but it also changes power, expectations, responsibility, and the experience of workers.
runbook.transition: Let’s test your instincts before we build a framework.

steps.label: 🗳️ QUICK JUDGMENT
steps.title: Would You Let AI Do This?
steps.lead: Make your own call before you hear anyone else.
choices: Summarize a meeting and assign action items
Recommend who should receive a promotion
steps.studentTask: Select the workplace uses you would allow AI to help with. Be ready to explain where your comfort changes.
steps.roomInstruction: WHAT WOULD YOU LET AI HELP DO?

runbook.say: These are all workplace AI uses. The interesting part is not whether AI can do them. The interesting part is what happens when the stakes rise.
runbook.askNext: What changed between the easiest task to delegate and the hardest one?
runbook.watchFor: Consequences, fairness, explainability, sensitive information, reversibility, and who owns the decision.
runbook.advanceWhen: Most students have responded and at least two students explain different boundaries.
runbook.landHere: The higher the consequence, the stronger the case for evidence, safeguards, and human authority.
runbook.transition: Now let’s use one pathway for analyzing any workplace AI case.

steps.label: 🧭 FRAMEWORK
steps.title: One Pathway for the Whole Session
steps.lead: Workplace Task → AI Assistance → Worker Impact → Organizational Risk → Responsible Workplace Practice
steps.studentTask: Use this pathway for every activity today—and later in your discussion post.
steps.roomInstruction: TASK → AI → WORKER → RISK → RESPONSIBLE PRACTICE

runbook.say: This is the same pathway you will use in the discussion. We are going to practice it before you write.
runbook.askNext: Which part of this pathway is easiest to ignore when people get excited about efficiency?
runbook.watchFor: Worker impact and organizational risk being omitted when students focus only on the tool.
runbook.advanceWhen: Students can restate the pathway in their own words.
runbook.landHere: Responsible AI analysis connects the technical use to the people affected and the organization’s responsibility.
runbook.transition: Now apply it to a job you may actually have.

steps.label: 🧠 SOLO AUDIT
steps.title: My Future Job Audit
steps.lead: Choose one job or field you may enter. What should AI do—and what should stay human?
steps.studentTask: Choose one future job. Identify 3–5 tasks. For each, decide: AI mostly does it, Human + AI together, or Human remains primarily responsible. Submit one task where human judgment matters most and explain why.
steps.roomInstruction: AI DOES · HUMAN + AI · HUMAN OWNS
steps.visualCaption: Do not protect a task only because 'that is how it has always been done.'

runbook.say: Work independently first. I want your judgment before your team influences it.
runbook.askNext: Are you keeping a task human because a person truly adds value—or because that is how the job has always been done?
runbook.watchFor: Students distinguishing routine production from judgment, relationships, exceptions, accountability, and context.
runbook.advanceWhen: Most students have submitted one task plus a reason.
runbook.landHere: AI may remove, shrink, or reshape tasks without removing the need for human judgment.
runbook.transition: Now compare your boundary with someone else’s.

steps.label: 🤝 TEAM CHALLENGE
steps.title: Redesign the Job
steps.lead: It is 2028. Your organization has powerful AI tools. Redesign a role without creating irresponsible automation.
steps.studentTask: Teams of 3–5: choose a role. Decide AI DOES / HUMAN DOES / HUMAN CHECKS. Name one task that shrinks, one human skill that becomes more valuable, and one decision you would NOT automate. Submit your team's one-sentence redesign.
steps.roomInstruction: AI DOES · HUMAN DOES · HUMAN CHECKS
steps.visualCaption: Maximum useful AI without irresponsible automation.

runbook.say: Your goal is not to protect every existing task. Your goal is to design a better job while protecting people and preserving meaningful human responsibility.
runbook.askNext: What is the one thing your team would explicitly refuse to automate—and why?
runbook.watchFor: Teams using vague 'human checks it' language. Push them to say what the human verifies and whether they can override.
runbook.advanceWhen: Each team has a redesign and one non-automated decision.
runbook.landHere: Human oversight only matters when it is specific and when the human has authority to question, correct, or override.
runbook.transition: You now have the raw material for your discussion post.

steps.label: ✍️ DISCUSSION POST
steps.title: Complete Your Initial Post
steps.lead: Turn today’s analysis into the actual AI in the Workplace discussion.
steps.studentTask: Open Canvas → Discussion / Activity | AI in the Workplace. Write and submit your initial post. Use one specific scenario, the workplace reasoning pathway, at least two perspectives, one benefit, one risk/limitation, one responsible action, and a closing question.
steps.visualCaption: Specific example · pathway · 2 perspectives · benefit · risk · responsible action · closing question

runbook.say: This is not prep time. This is assignment-completion time. Use the thinking you already did so you do not have to recreate it later.
runbook.askNext: Before you submit: can someone else clearly see who benefits, who may be disadvantaged, and what the organization should do?
runbook.watchFor: Students writing generally instead of using a specific scenario; missing second perspective; missing responsible action; missing closing question.
runbook.advanceWhen: Most students have submitted their initial post in Canvas.
runbook.landHere: A strong post makes the reasoning visible from workplace task to responsible workplace practice.
runbook.transition: Now use your classmates’ posts to widen your thinking.

steps.label: 💬 REPLY #1
steps.title: Respond to a Different Perspective
steps.lead: Your reply should add thinking—not just agreement.
steps.studentTask: Read a classmate’s post and submit Reply #1. Compare perspectives, add missing context, ask a responsible-use question, respectfully challenge the reasoning, connect to human judgment, or add a new example.

runbook.say: Pick a post that gives you something to think about—not necessarily one you already agree with.
runbook.askNext: What can you add that the original post does not already say?
runbook.watchFor: Replies that merely praise or repeat. Prompt students to compare, question, extend, or challenge.
runbook.advanceWhen: Most students have submitted their first reply.
runbook.landHere: Discussion becomes valuable when a reply changes, sharpens, or expands the reasoning.
runbook.transition: One more reply—this time choose a different scenario or perspective.

steps.label: 💬 REPLY #2
steps.title: Add a Second Perspective
steps.lead: Choose a different classmate or a different workplace scenario.
steps.studentTask: Submit Reply #2 to a different classmate. Add a perspective, missing context, risk, safeguard, or human-judgment question that moves the discussion forward.

runbook.say: Your second reply should add something new. If your first reply focused on fairness, maybe this one focuses on accountability, training, privacy, job quality, or human review.
runbook.askNext: What did this classmate notice that your own post did not?
runbook.watchFor: Students choosing the same perspective twice or repeating themselves.
runbook.advanceWhen: Most students have submitted the second reply.
runbook.landHere: Multiple perspectives are not decoration; they change what responsible workplace practice looks like.
runbook.transition: Let’s finish by identifying what makes a human valuable in an AI-enabled workplace.

steps.label: 🏁 CLOSE
steps.title: If Everyone Has AI, What Makes You Valuable?
steps.lead: AI literacy is not only knowing how to use the tool. It is knowing what to delegate, what to verify, and what humans must still own.
steps.studentTask: Submit one sentence: One human skill I need to strengthen because of AI is ______ because ______.

runbook.say: If everyone can access AI, your advantage is not simply having the tool. It is knowing what to delegate, how to judge what comes back, and when the human needs to take control.
runbook.askNext: What human skill becomes more valuable—not less valuable—because AI is everywhere?
runbook.watchFor: Judgment, communication, domain knowledge, verification, creativity, empathy, problem framing, adaptability, accountability.
runbook.landHere: AI literacy in the workplace is the ability to use AI without giving away human responsibility.
runbook.transition: You should leave today with the discussion completed and a clearer view of your own future work.
